claim: Many species perform rapid limb movements as part of their elaborate courtship displays.
source: Many species perform rapid limb movements as part of their elaborate courtship displays.
evidence: This is a general statement about animal behavior that draws from established scientific knowledge about courtship displays.

claim: Muscle performance is constrained by trade-offs between contraction speed and force.
source: However, because muscle performance is constrained by trade-offs between contraction speed and force, it is unclear how animals evolve the ability to produce both unusually fast appendage movement and limb force needed for locomotion.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Rome et al., 1999 and Young and Rome, 2001 elsewhere in the manuscript, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Golden-collared manakins and red-capped manakins have evolved 'superfast' contractile kinetics in their main humeral retractor muscle.
source: Our results show that the two taxa that perform exceptionally fast wing displays have evolved 'superfast' contractile kinetics in their main humeral retractor muscle.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: The two muscles that generate the majority of aerodynamic force for flight show unmodified contractile kinetics.
source: By contrast, the two muscles that generate the majority of aerodynamic force for flight show unmodified contractile kinetics.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing muscle kinetics across species.

claim: Muscle-specific adaptations in contractile speed allow certain birds to circumvent the intrinsic trade-off between muscular speed and force.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that muscle-specific adaptations in contractile speed allow certain birds to circumvent the intrinsic trade-off between muscular speed and force, and thereby use their forelimbs for both rapid gestural displays and powered locomotion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing differential muscle adaptations.

claim: Signal evolution in animals has produced a variety of unique and unusual displays, including elaborate physical routines performed for social communication and advertisement.
source: Signal evolution in animals has produced a variety of unique and unusual displays, including the elaborate physical routines performed for social communication and advertisement (Beehler and Pruett-Jones, 1983; Prum, 1990; Masonjones and Lewis, 1996; Voigt et al., 2001; Hogg and Forbes, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Little is understood about how elaborate physical displays evolve.
source: Little is understood about how these displays evolve, and their emergence represents a functional feat in animal design (Fuxjager and Schlinger, 2015; Irschick et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations indicating a gap in scientific knowledge.

claim: Motor performance is constrained by a trade-off between muscle contraction force and speed.
source: However, because motor performance is constrained by a trade-off between muscle contraction force and speed (Rome et al., 1999; Young and Rome, 2001), limb muscles should in theory be unable to generate both the swift appendage movements incorporated in showy physical displays and the force needed to drive locomotion (Young and Rome, 2001; Rome and Lindstedt, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research on muscle physiology.

claim: Trade-offs between muscle force and contraction speed exist in the wing muscles of birds within the size range studied.
source: Trade-offs between muscle force and contraction speed clearly exist in the wing muscles of birds within this size range (Biewener, 2011; Biewener and Roberts, 2000; Biewener et al., 1992; Dial and Biewener, 1993; Hedrick et al., 2003), and evidence suggests that such muscles maintain sufficient force-generating abilities to power flight and regulate flying speeds (Biewener et al., 1992; Dial and Biewener, 1993; Hedrick et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research on bird wing muscle physiology.

claim: Male golden-collared manakins perform roll-snaps, whereby they hit their wings together above their backs at ≈60 Hz to produce a loud mechanical sonation.
source: For example, male golden-collared manakins perform roll-snaps, whereby they hit their wings together above their backs at ≈60 Hz to produce a loud mechanical sonation (Fusani et al., 2007; Fuxjager et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior kinematic studies.

claim: Roll-snap behavior is performed by elevating the opened wings and then by repeatedly retracting the wings to force the wrists to collide in quick succession.
source: Kinematic analyses suggest that this behavior is performed by elevating the opened (extended) wings and then by repeatedly retracting the wings to force the wrists to collide in quick succession (Bostwick and Prum, 2003; Fusani et al., 2007; Fuxjager et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior kinematic analyses.

claim: Male red-capped manakins produce a wing sonation called a clap, in which the wings are laterally extended slightly above the body and then immediately retracted back to the sides.
source: Likewise, male red-capped manakins produce a similar wing sonation called a clap, in which the wings are laterally extended slightly above the body and then immediately retracted back to the sides (Bostwick and Prum, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Claps are produced in rapid succession, with the wing-extension and wing-retraction phases occurring at ≈45 Hz.
source: Claps are also produced in rapid succession, with the wing-extension and wing-retraction phases occurring at ≈45 Hz (Bostwick and Prum, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The wing oscillation frequencies used for courtship displays in golden-collared and red-capped manakins exceed those that similarly sized birds use for flight (≈25–30 Hz).
source: In both species, the wing oscillation frequencies used for courtship displays exceed those that similarly sized birds use for flight (≈25–30 Hz) (Donovan et al., 2013; Pennycuick, 2001); thus, the forelimb motor system is likely modified to actuate courtship movements, while preserving the force-generating ability needed to drive powered locomotion.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on bird flight frequencies, with an inference about motor system modification.

claim: The supracoracoideus (SC) raises the wing by elevating the humerus.
source: (i) the supracoracoideus (SC), which raises the wing by elevating the humerus; (ii) the pectoralis (PEC), which lowers the wing by depressing the humerus, and (iii) the scapulohumeralis caudalis (SH), which retracts the wing via the humerus [Figure 1B; Biewener, 2011, Dial, 1992, Dial et al., 1991].
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The pectoralis (PEC) lowers the wing by depressing the humerus.
source: (i) the supracoracoideus (SC), which raises the wing by elevating the humerus; (ii) the pectoralis (PEC), which lowers the wing by depressing the humerus, and (iii) the scapulohumeralis caudalis (SH), which retracts the wing via the humerus [Figure 1B; Biewener, 2011, Dial, 1992, Dial et al., 1991].
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The scapulohumeralis caudalis (SH) retracts the wing via the humerus.
source: (i) the supracoracoideus (SC), which raises the wing by elevating the humerus; (ii) the pectoralis (PEC), which lowers the wing by depressing the humerus, and (iii) the scapulohumeralis caudalis (SH), which retracts the wing via the humerus [Figure 1B; Biewener, 2011, Dial, 1992, Dial et al., 1991].
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The SH acts as the main wing retractor and generates the least aerodynamic force necessary for powered flight.
source: Because the SH acts as the main wing retractor and generates the least aerodynamic force necessary for powered flight, we predict that its contractile kinetics are significantly increased in golden-collared and red-capped manakins, compared to the SC and PEC.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge of muscle biomechanics and is used to support a prediction.

claim: Blue-crowned manakins produce an elaborate physical display without rapid wing-snaps or wing-flicks.
source: The first of these is the blue-crowned manakin (Lepidothrix coronata), which is a close relative of the aforementioned manakins and produces an elaborate physical display without rapid wing-snaps or wing-flicks (Durães, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Dusky antbirds inhabit the same niche as the manakins and produce elaborate vocalizations in lieu of a physical display.
source: The second species is the dusky antbird (Cercomarca tyrannica), which inhabits the same niche as the manakins described above but produces elaborate vocalizations in lieu of a physical display (Morton and Derrickson, 1996; Morton, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: House wrens sing to attract mates and do not produce a robust physical display.
source: The last bird is the house wren (Troglodytes aedon), a more distant relative within the same avian order that sings to attract mates and does not produce a robust physical display (Johnson and Kermott, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There was no significant difference in percent relaxation values between the first and second 20 Hz stimulation events.
source: Overall, we found no significant difference in percent relaxation values between these two separate stimulation events (Table 1; all p values ≥0.18).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data presented in Table 1.

claim: The muscles were functionally intact throughout the twitch frequency recording sessions.
source: These results therefore indicate that the muscles were functionally intact throughout the twitch frequency recording sessions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing no difference in muscle relaxation between first and second 20 Hz stimulations.

claim: Muscle stimulations actuated wing movement.
source: Indeed, we found that this was the case, as the muscle stimulations that we administered actuated wing movement.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental procedure.

claim: High contraction-relaxation cycling rates translate to corresponding high frequency wing oscillations.
source: These data indicate that high contraction-relaxation cycling rates translate to corresponding high frequency wing oscillations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observing wing movements during high-frequency stimulations.

claim: Non-linear regression models characterizing muscle contraction speeds in response to varying stimulation frequencies differed significantly among taxa for each muscle.
source: For each muscle, models differed significantly among taxa (Figure 3A,B and C; PEC: F16,130 = 2.50, p =0.0023; SC: F16,140 = 5.50, p<0.001.; SH: SC: F16,134 = 15.68, p<0.001).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is performance variability in the PEC, SC, and SH muscles across species.
source: This suggests that there is performance variability in these muscles, and we suspect that such results underlie functional differences in the way in which the forelimb musculature controls rates of wing flapping.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical differences in muscle models across species.

claim: For both the PEC and the SC, half-relaxation frequencies averaged ≈50 Hz and were indistinguishable among species.
source: For both the PEC and the SC, half-relaxation frequencies averaged ≈50 Hz and were indistinguishable among species (Figure 3D, PEC: F4,10 = 0.85, p = 0.53; Figure 3E, SC: F4,11 = 1.74, p = 0.39).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: In the SH, the half-relaxation frequencies differed significantly among taxa.
source: By contrast, in the SH, the half-relaxation frequencies differed significantly among taxa (Figure 3F, F4,11 = 10.09, p = 0.0011), and post-hoc analysis of this effect showed these frequency measures were significantly higher in both golden-collared and red-capped manakins compared to the other three species in the study (Figure 3G and Table 2; golden-collared: SNK post-hoc tests, q≥6.17, p<0.01; red-capped: SNK post-hoc tests, q≥3.64, p<0.05).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Table 2.

claim: SH half-relaxation frequencies were significantly higher in both golden-collared and red-capped manakins compared to the other three species.
source: By contrast, in the SH, the half-relaxation frequencies differed significantly among taxa (Figure 3F, F4,11 = 10.09, p = 0.0011), and post-hoc analysis of this effect showed these frequency measures were significantly higher in both golden-collared and red-capped manakins compared to the other three species in the study (Figure 3G and Table 2; golden-collared: SNK post-hoc tests, q≥6.17, p<0.01; red-capped: SNK post-hoc tests, q≥3.64, p<0.05).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Table 2.

claim: Estimates of SH half-relaxation frequencies in golden-collared and red-capped manakins were exceptionally high, coming in at ≈100 Hz and ≈80 Hz, respectively.
source: Estimates of these two birds' SH half-relaxation frequencies were exceptionally high, coming in at ≈100 Hz and ≈80 Hz, respectively.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data from the regression models.

claim: The SH half-relaxation frequencies between golden-collared and red-capped manakins were statistically indistinguishable.
source: Moreover, the SH half-relaxation frequencies between golden-collared and red-capped manakins were statistically indistinguishable (Figure 3F and Table 2; SNK post-hoc tests, q = 2.52, p>0.05).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Table 2.

claim: The SH in golden-collared manakins achieves on average ≈85% relaxation in response to stimulation frequencies of around 95 Hz.
source: In the case of the golden-collared manakin, we found that the SH achieves on average ≈85% relaxation in response to stimulation frequencies of around 95 Hz.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data from the regression models.

claim: The SH in red-capped manakins achieves ≈85% relaxation in response to stimulation frequencies of roughly 70 Hz.
source: In the red-capped manakin, the SH achieves the same amount of mean relaxation in response to stimulation frequencies of roughly 70 Hz.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data from the regression models.

claim: The SH is more than capable of driving the natural wing oscillations that make up each species' wing display.
source: The observation of concurrent wing movements at these stimulation frequencies (see above) shows that these changes in muscle length can actuate humeral retraction; thus, our results suggest that the SH is more than capable of driving the natural wing oscillations that make up each species' wing display (Bostwick and Prum, 2003; Fusani et al., 2007; Fuxjager et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data showing muscle relaxation at high frequencies and observed wing movements, combined with citations to prior kinematic studies.

claim: The rapid kinetics of the SH suggest that this muscle features specializations that are similar to those of so-called 'superfast' muscles.
source: Such rapid kinetics of the SH suggest that this muscle features specializations that are similar to those of so-called 'superfast' muscles (Rome et al., 1996; Elemans et al., 2008; Elemans et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data on SH kinetics, supported by citations to prior research on superfast muscles.

claim: The SH is one of the main actuators of the rapid forearm movements that are incorporated into golden-collared and red-capped manakin displays.
source: We hypothesize that the SH is one of the main actuators of the rapid forearm movements that are incorporated into golden-collared and red-capped manakin displays.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from kinematic studies and the biomechanical role of the SH.

claim: Golden-collared manakins generate their wing sonations by moving their forelimbs at frequencies of 55–63 Hz.
source: Kinematic studies suggest that these species generate their wing sonations by moving their forelimbs at frequencies of 55–63 Hz and 45 Hz, respectively (Bostwick and Prum, 2003; Fusani et al., 2007; Fuxjager et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior kinematic studies.

claim: Red-capped manakins generate their wing sonations by moving their forelimbs at frequencies of 45 Hz.
source: Kinematic studies suggest that these species generate their wing sonations by moving their forelimbs at frequencies of 55–63 Hz and 45 Hz, respectively (Bostwick and Prum, 2003; Fusani et al., 2007; Fuxjager et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior kinematic studies.

claim: The wing sonation rates in golden-collared and red-capped manakins fall well within the range of stimulation frequencies at which significant recovery of the SH is observed (at least 85%).
source: Our results show that these rates fall well within the range of stimulation frequencies at which significant recovery of the SH is observed (at least 85%), and we find that individual stimulations are accompanied by observable wing movements.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing experimental data on muscle relaxation with prior kinematic data on display frequencies.

claim: The bulk of the rapid forearm movement in manakin displays is driven by repetitive humeral retraction.
source: In addition, these same kinematic studies suggest that the bulk of the rapid forearm movement is driven by repetitive humeral retraction, and such movement of the wing is fully consistent with the biomechanical role of the SH (Dial, 1992; Dial et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior kinematic studies and knowledge of muscle biomechanics.

claim: The SH is the main muscle driving display production in both golden-collared and red-capped manakins.
source: Thus, these data collectively suggest that the SH is the main muscle driving display production in both animals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data on muscle kinetics, kinematic studies, and knowledge of muscle biomechanics.

claim: Sexual selection likely favored the emergence of rapid contractility in the SH.
source: Since the elaborate displays of manakins are used for courtship and male-male rivalry (Bostwick and Prum, 2003; McDonald et al., 2001; Barske et al., 2011), sexual selection likely favored the emergence of rapid contractility in the SH.
evidence: This is an inference based on citations about display function and evolutionary reasoning.

claim: The superfast kinetics of the SH make it the fastest vertebrate limb muscle currently known, at least with respect to measures of twitch contraction.
source: To this end, these superfast kinetics make the SH in these two birds the fastest vertebrate limb muscles currently known, at least with respect to measures of twitch contraction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data on SH kinetics compared to knowledge of other vertebrate limb muscles.

claim: The SH contractile kinetics markedly exceed the typical wing-beat frequencies during flight (25–30 Hz) for birds of similar size.
source: Moreover, we know that these frequencies markedly exceed the typical wing-beat frequencies during flight (25–30 Hz) for birds of similar size (Donovan et al., 2013; Pennycuick, 2001), which again implies that sexual selection has positvely favored the emergence of an extreme muscle phenotype to accommodate the evolution of an equally extreme behavior.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data on SH kinetics and citations to prior research on bird flight frequencies, with an inference about sexual selection.

claim: Females preferentially mate with males that perform certain display maneuvers at fractions-of-a-second faster speeds.
source: Studies in golden-collared manakins suggest that females preferentially mate with males that perform certain display maneuvers at fractions-of-a-second faster speeds (Barske et al., 2011; 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on female mate choice.

claim: Other wing muscles, like the 'slower' SC and PEC, may also contribute to display production by helping position the wings.
source: Therefore, one intriguing possibility is that other wing muscles, like the 'slower' SC and PEC, also contribute to display production by helping position the wings (Fusani et al., 2014; Schlinger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Display speed itself may be constrained by neural circuits that integrate and/or coordinate the activation of numerous forearm motor units.
source: If this is the case, then display speed itself may be constrained by neural circuits that integrate and/or coordinate the activation of numerous forearm motor units, as opposed to only the speed of the SH.
evidence: This is speculation based on inference from the potential role of multiple muscles in display production.

claim: Muscle twitch speeds are modified in the SH, but not the SC or PEC in golden-collared and red-capped manakins.
source: This, in effect, is rooted in our finding that muscle twitch speeds are modified in the SH, but not the SC or PEC.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data comparing muscle kinetics across species.

claim: The SC and PEC maintain half-relaxation rates of ≈50 Hz, which are similar to the half-relaxation frequencies of all three muscles in the non-wing-displaying blue-crowned manakin, dusky antbird, and house wren.
source: Rather, the latter two muscles maintain half-relaxation rates of ≈50 Hz, which are similar to the half-relaxation frequencies of all three muscles in the non-wing-displaying blue-crowned manakin, dusky antbird, and house wren.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data comparing muscle kinetics across species.

claim: In golden-collared and red-capped manakins, the SC and PEC twitch speeds are largely conserved.
source: Thus, in golden-collared and red-capped manakins, the SC and PEC twitch speeds are largely conserved, which means that the ability of these muscles to generate aerodynamic force needed for powered flight is not compromised by the mutually exclusive ability to contract rapidly (Rome et al., 1999; Young and Rome, 2001).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data on muscle kinetics, supported by citations to prior research on muscle trade-offs.

claim: Flight in golden-collared and red-capped manakins is unencumbered.
source: Flight in these two manakins is therefore unencumbered (Moore et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research on manakin flight performance.

claim: The SH contributes to aerodynamic force by adjusting the wings' angle of attack, area, and/or camber.
source: To this end, this model is consistent with the biomechanical role of the SH, which contributes to aerodynamic force by adjusting the wings' angle of attack, area, and/or camber (Dial, 1992; Dial et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on muscle biomechanics.

claim: The SH likely contributes least to the generation of power for flight.
source: The SH therefore likely contributes least to the generation of power for flight, and thus presents more opportunity for evolutionary modification without severely compromising flight ability.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of muscle biomechanics and evolutionary reasoning.

claim: This is the first glimpse into how evolution might circumvent trade-offs between muscle contraction speed and force generation to favor the emergence of rapid appendage displays, while maintaining normal locomotion.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first glimpse into how evolution might circumvent trade-offs between muscle contraction speed and force generation to favor the emergence of rapid appendage displays, while maintaining normal locomotion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Both golden-collared and red-capped manakins are strong fliers, relative to other similarly sized tropical birds.
source: Past work shows that both golden-collared and red-capped manakins are strong fliers, relative to other similarly sized tropical birds (Moore et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Dramatically enhancing the contraction speed of the SH does not altogether impede or diminish locomotion.
source: This result indicates that dramatically enhancing the contraction speed of the SH does not altogether impede or diminish locomotion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited research showing that manakins are strong fliers.

claim: Both golden-collared and red-capped manakins produce a muffled fluttering sound when they fly.
source: However, studies have noted that both of these species produce a muffled fluttering sound when they fly (Bostwick and Prum, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: It is unclear if the muffled fluttering sound produced during flight is a sexual signal or a by-product of physiological and/or biomechanical adaptations that enable elaborate courtship maneuvering.
source: It is unclear if this sound, like the other sonations these birds produce, is a sexual signal, or whether it is a by-product of physiological and/or biomechanical adaptations that enable elaborate courtship maneuvering.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of the flight sound.

claim: The ability of the SH to appropriately control wing positioning might be altered by this muscle's performance shift.
source: If the latter is true, then our results might provide a mechanism for such action, as the ability of the SH to appropriately control wing positioning (Dial, 1992) might be altered by this muscle's performance shift.
evidence: This is speculation based on inference from experimental data and cited knowledge of muscle function.

claim: Adult male manakins were captured via passive mist netting at their respective breeding leks.
source: Adult male manakins were captured via passive mist netting at their respective breeding leks (golden-collared manakins, n = 3, red-capped manakins, n = 3, blue crowned manakins, n = 3).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Adult male dusky antbirds and house wrens were captured from their breeding territories by luring individuals into the net with conspecific playback.
source: At the same time, adult male dusky antbirds (n = 4) and house wrens (n = 3) were captured from their breeding territories by luring individuals into the net with conspecific playback.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Birds were immediately transported to the laboratory for muscle recordings, after which they were euthanized with an overdose of isoflurane.
source: Birds were immediately transported to our nearby laboratory for muscle recordings (see below), after which they were euthanized with an overdose of isoflurane and their tissues were removed for another study.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: The testes of each specimen were inspected to verify that they were enlarged and that the individual was in reproductive condition.
source: We inspected the testes of each specimen to verify that they were enlarged and that the individual was in reproductive condition.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: The work was conducted from March to April in Gamboa, Panama at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI).
source: The work was conducted from March to April in Gamboa, Panama at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Contraction-relaxation speed within a stimulus period was assessed by measuring the degree to which each muscle relaxed relative to its un-stimulated length in response to different frequencies of electrical stimulation.
source: Contraction-relaxation speed within a stimulus period was assessed by measuring the degree to which each muscle relaxed relative to its un-stimulated length (i.e., percent recovery) in response to different frequencies of electrical stimulation (see Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: All muscles were subjected to stimulation frequencies of 10 Hz, 20 Hz, 30 Hz, 40 Hz, 50 Hz, 60 Hz, 70 Hz, 80 Hz, 90 Hz, and 100 Hz.
source: All muscles were subjected to the following stimulation frequencies: 10 Hz, 20 Hz, 30 Hz, 40 Hz, 50 Hz, 60 Hz, 70 Hz, 80 Hz, 90 Hz, and 100 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Each stimulation train consisted of 10 separate pulses.
source: Each stimulation train consisted of 10 separate pulses.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Pulse duration was set to 1 ms, and the pulse current was set between 0.5–0.8 mA.
source: Pulse duration was set to 1 ms, and the pulse current was set between 0.5–0.8 mA.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Stimulation trains were always delivered from low frequency (10 Hz) to high frequency (100 Hz).
source: Stimulation trains were always delivered from low frequency (10 Hz) to high frequency (100 Hz).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Subsequent stimulation trains were spaced 1 min apart from each other to allow the muscle to temporarily rest.
source: We space subsequent stimulation trains 1 min apart from each other to allow the muscle to temporarily rest.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: A second 20 Hz stimulation train was delivered 1 min after the series' final 100 Hz stimulation to confirm that results were not confounded by damage or exhaustion of the muscle.
source: To confirm that our results were not confounded by damage or exhaustion of the muscle in response to repeated stimulations, we delivered a second 20 Hz stimulation train 1 min after the series' final 100 Hz stimulation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Muscle twitch speeds were recorded in situ.
source: Muscle twitch speeds were recorded in situ (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Birds were restrained on a soft foam pad that was securely attached to the surgical bench.
source: For all preparations, birds were restrained on a soft foam pad that was securely attached to the surgical bench.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Birds were anesthetized with isoflurane (2–4% in O2).
source: Birds were then anesthetized with isoflurane (2–4% in O2).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: The PEC and SH were exposed by cutting a small (1 cm) incision in the skin and gently pushing apart the skin.
source: To prepare the PEC and SH, we first cut a small (1 cm) incision in the skin. We then exposed the moist surface of the muscle by gently pushing apart the skin.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: The muscles were implanted with the stripped ends (1–2 mm) of two insulated silver wire electrodes (diameter: 0.14 mm).
source: Once the muscle was in clear view, we implanted it with the stripped ends (1–2 mm) of two insulated silver wire electrodes (diameter: 0.14 mm).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: A stainless steel hook (0.1 mm diameter) was fastened to the muscle directly adjacent to the implanted electrodes and connected through a monofilament line to a force transducer.
source: We next fastened a stainless steel hook (0.1 mm diameter) to the muscle directly adjacent to the implanted electrodes. This hook was connected through a monofilament line to a force transducer (Model FT03, Grass Technology, RI, USA), which was tightly clamped to a heavy stand (≈6 kg).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: A drop of normal avian saline (0.9%) was placed over the exposed muscles to prevent tissue desiccation during the recording session.
source: As soon as this preparation was completed, we placed a drop of normal avian saline (0.9%) over the exposed muscles to prevent tissues desiccation during the recording session.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: All surgical preparations occurred at room temperature, which was similar to the outside ambient temperature (≈30°C).
source: All surgical preparations occurred at room temperature, which was similar to the outside ambient temperature (≈30°C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: The SC was prepared by cutting a small (1.5 cm) incision in the skin above the furcula and gently moving aside the underlying fat-pad to expose the inter-clavicular air-sac.
source: First, we cut a small (1.5 cm) incision in the skin above the furcula. We then gently moved aside the underlying fat-pad and exposed the inter-clavicular air-sac.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: The membrane of the inter-clavicular air-sac was carefully moved to the side to gain access to the SC, taking great caution not to puncture it.
source: To gain access to the SC, we carefully moved the membrane of this air-sac to the side, taking great caution not to puncture it.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: For the SC, the hook from the force transducer was attached to the bird's elbow rather than directly to the muscle.
source: Given the deep (and difficult) position of the SC, it was not possible to fasten the hook from the force transducer directly to the muscle for twitch speed recordings. Instead, we attached the hook to the bird's elbow, and recorded the action of the stimulated SC as movement of the wing.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: The stimulator and force transducer were connected to a laptop through an A-D converter.
source: Both the stimulator and force transducer were connected to a laptop through an A-D converter (Model NI USB-6212, National Instruments, TX, USA).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Complete muscle relaxation (100% relaxation) occurred when the extra tension detected by the force transducer in response to stimulation was fully relieved.
source: Complete muscle relaxation (100% relaxation) occurred when the extra tension detected by the force transducer in response to stimulation was fully relieved (i.e., the signal returned to its baseline level).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Partial muscle relaxation occurred when the extra tension placed on the force transducer in response to stimulation was less than fully relieved (i.e., summation occurred).
source: Partial muscle relaxation occurred when the extra tension placed on the force transducer in response to stimulation was less than fully relieved (i.e., summation occurred).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: For each stimulation train, the percent recovery values for the first eight stimulations were averaged.
source: For each stimulation train, we averaged the percent recovery values for the first eight stimulations.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Averaging the first eight stimulations corresponds to similar numbers of wing-oscillations that golden-collared and red-capped manakins use in their forelimb displays.
source: This corresponds to similar numbers of wing-oscillations that golden-collared and red-capped manakins use in their forelimb displays (Bostwick and Prum, 2003; Fuxjager et al., 2013).

claim: Percent recoveries obtained from 20 Hz stimulations administered at the onset and after the experimental series were compared using paired t-tests.
source: For each muscle, we compared the percent recoveries obtained from 20 Hz stimulations administered at the onset and after the experimental series using paired t-tests.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: In red-capped manakins, 20 Hz stimulations elicited 100% recovery in all cases, so statistics could not be performed.
source: One exception to this analysis occurred in red-capped manakins, as 20 Hz stimulations elicited 100% recovery in all cases. Variation across biological replicates is therefore 0.0, which means that statistics cannot be performed.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: The four-parameter logistic non-linear regression model characterizes data that form a reverse sigmoidal curve and is widely used to assess a variety of biological functions.
source: This type of model characterizes data that form a reverse sigmoidal curve, and it is widely used to assess a variety of biological functions [e.g., Kent et al., 1972, Johnson et al., 2003].

claim: Model thresholds were constrained at or below 100% (maximum possible percent relaxation) and model saturations at or above 0% (minimum possible percent recovery).
source: We constrained model thresholds at or below 100% (maximum possible percent relaxation) and model saturations at or above 0% (minimum possible percent recovery).

source: Each model produced an estimated inflection point (± 1 SEM), which represents the muscle's half-relaxation frequency.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: The half-relaxation frequency is defined as the stimulation frequency at which the muscle's average recovery equals half of its predicted functional range.
source: This metric is defined as the stimulation frequency at which the muscle's average recovery equals half of its predicted functional range.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: The half-relaxation point represents a change in muscle length that is still highly effective in actuating movement of the appendage (wing).
source: The half-relaxation point is biologically significant, in that it represents a change in muscle length that is still highly effective in actuating movement of the appendage (wing).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the biological significance of the half-relaxation frequency metric.

claim: At the level of muscle fusions associated with the half-relaxation frequency, generation of the display behavior is still highly feasible.
source: Thus, at the level of muscle fusions associated with the half-relaxation frequency, generation of the display behavior is still highly feasible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biological significance of the half-relaxation frequency.

claim: Models and their estimates of half-relaxation frequency were statistically compared only within muscle type.
source: To this end, we statistically compared models and their estimates of half-relaxation frequency only within muscle type, considering that differences in the preparations of the separate muscles might affect model parameters.

claim: Extra sum-of-squares tests were used to compare models across species.
source: Therefore, we used extra sum-of-squares tests to compare models across species and one-way ANOVAs to compare half-relaxation frequencies across species.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: One-way ANOVAs were used to compare half-relaxation frequencies across species.
source: Therefore, we used extra sum-of-squares tests to compare models across species and one-way ANOVAs to compare half-relaxation frequencies across species.

claim: Significant effects from ANOVAs were followed by Student-Newman-Keuls (SNK) post-hoc comparisons to control for multiple pairwise contrasts.
source: Significant effects from ANOVAs were followed by Student-Newman-Keuls (SNK) post-hoc comparisons to control for multiple pairwise contrasts.
